cells.literature: [L] Personalised designs are proposed to show the student's own work when students must justify their choices or verify AI output against their own research [R73], [R15], but these claims were not tested or rest on student self-report [R71]. Stronger evidence appears when personalisation is applied to questioning: viva questions generated from each student's own project reached QWK 0.782 agreement with human grades [S156], and experts rated text-specific open-ended comprehension items highly for checking understanding [R11].
cells.dataset: [D] In one AI course, students averaged 94.8% on AI-permitted take-home assignments but 86.3% on proctored exams [D24], and assignment marks did not respond to the share of verbatim AI-authored content [J1].
cells.interpretation: [I] A personalised artefact alone says little about individual understanding; credibility depends on adding explanation, justification or questioning tied to the student's own work.
cells.conflicts: Most claims for the task itself are untested proposals or self-report [R73], [R71]; code-specific verification questions in R77 were not evaluated [R77]. S156 and R11 concern personalised questioning rather than personalised tasks.

cells.literature: [L] Authors argue that any homework can be passed to an AI tool, and that students can prompt AI to simplify code so it looks like novice work [R73]; R15 notes that authenticity alone does not protect integrity [R15]. Lecturers found personal reflective statements especially open to AI misuse [S208], and practitioners doubted that portfolios resist GenAI [R24]. Resistance was reported only where tasks used application-specific commands that general LLMs are not trained on, and this rests on student self-report [R71].
cells.dataset: [D] Under a best-of-8 adversary, item-format features explained little of AI resistance (pseudo R2 0.12-0.15), while resistance varied between courses from 4.3% to 47.4%: security does not reside in question format [J3]. GPT-4 fully answered 85.6% of CS questions when the best of 8 prompts could be chosen [D03].
cells.interpretation: [I] Personalising or contextualising the question is not in itself a security measure, and any resistance that depends on what current models do not know is likely to be temporary.
cells.conflicts: R71 students rated custom commands as a strong barrier to copy-paste (B2 4.57), but this is self-report with no misconduct data [R71]. Delegation to AI was lowest in applied scenarios requiring explanations, but this is descriptive only (12 units) [J2]. The EPFL data use 2023 models and exam-style items, not personalised tasks [D03], [J3].

cells.literature: [L] Personalisation does not by itself establish who produced the work: detecting AI-generated code was described as challenging and often impractical [R73], and the only misconduct check in R15 relied on detectors its authors call unreliable [R15]. GenAI declarations were judged ineffective, whereas named marking by tutors who know the students reportedly coincided with fewer misconduct cases [R24]. Reviews report that AI detectors are unreliable [R01], [R51].
cells.dataset: [D] In one course, within-assignment marks did not respond to the share of verbatim chatbot code in submissions (-1.0 points from 0% to 100% overlap, 95% CI -4.3 to +2.3) [J1].
cells.interpretation: [I] Authorship assurance has to come from paired measures such as process logs or questioning on the work, not from the personal content of the task.
cells.conflicts: R77 shows that activity logs detected most instructed plagiarism, including transcribed AI code (F1 91.93%), but this is process evidence rather than personalisation [R77].

cells.literature: [L] The GENESIS design matrix maps personalised authentic contexts to ICT graduate competencies [R04], and course-specific tasks are argued to preserve the trial-and-error and conceptual learning that copy-paste would bypass [R71], [R73]. Implemented personalised tasks were linked to computing benchmark expectations and AI-literacy aims [R15], [R20]. However, GenAI use can mean students demonstrate prompting skill rather than the targeted sub-skills [R51].
cells.dataset: [D] In one course, AI-permitted assignment marks bunched near the top and agreed only moderately with exam marks (rho = 0.53) [D25].
cells.interpretation: [I] Alignment is good when the personal or local context carries the intended reasoning, and weaker when personalisation only changes surface details of a product-focused task.
cells.conflicts: Alignment is argued rather than measured in all studies [R04], [R71].

cells.literature: [L] Personalised, authentic-context and real-life problem tasks are widely recommended as more valid [R04], [R01], [R03], and authentic tasks were the third most frequent change teachers suggested (n = 65) [R50]. Computing examples drew on realistic scenarios such as a customer-data GUI with messy names and addresses [R73], and students perceived AI-resistant tasks as more authentic tests of their ability [R71]. Tasks that permit GenAI were argued to fit workplaces where graduates will use it [R19], [R51].
cells.dataset: [D] Most capstone clients (7 of 11) wanted students to be supported to use GenAI [D20], although this figure may be inflated by the questionnaire framing [J5].
cells.interpretation: [I] Contextualised tasks with AI available resemble professional computing work, but the rating rests on recommendations and perceptions rather than measured authenticity.
cells.conflicts: R15 notes that authenticity alone does not protect integrity [R15]. AI-resistant variants that rely on custom commands [R71] or lecture-only edge cases [R73] may be less like practice where AI is available. Calibration C4: rating rests on author framing of designs, not on tested outcomes, so confidence is Low.

cells.literature: [L] Some personalised tasks required GenAI use and gave marks for checking AI output for completeness, bias and hallucinations [R15], or trained students to use tools constructively and reflect on that use [R20]. Others aim to make AI fail, through lecture-specific details [R73] or custom commands, where the author proposes mixing AI-easy and AI-hard tasks to build AI literacy [R71]. Frameworks place personal and contextual tasks in an 'Avoid' category separate from AI-integrated 'Adopt' tasks [R19].
cells.dataset: [D] In capstone students' own advice, the most frequent directives were 'Retain Understanding' (39.3%) and 'Reviewing Outputs' (29.2%) [D19].
cells.interpretation: [I] Performance depends on whether the design integrates AI with explicit critique or tries to keep AI out.
cells.conflicts: AI-integrated and AI-resistant versions of the type pull in opposite directions [R15], [R73].

cells.literature: [L] Personalised tasks became process-visible only when process requirements were added: R15 gave marks for search evidence, prompts, AI outputs and reflection [R15], and R20 required reflections showing tool use at each writing stage [R20]. Students in R71 suggested asking for explanations of the process leading to a result [R71].
cells.interpretation: [I] Personalisation itself exposes only the product; process visibility depends on pairing it with process evidence.
cells.conflicts: Lecturers found reflective statements especially open to AI misuse, so reflections may not reliably show process [S208].

cells.literature: [L] LLM generation can give each learner unique questions: 83% were instructor-acceptable at first generation, but difficulty varied by up to 30% and the platform broke at 300 concurrent users [R89]. A divergent topic per student ran in an 88-student module [R15], and project-specific viva questions were generated for over 250 students in 67 groups [S156]. Other personalised designs were tested only in classes of up to 30 students [R94] and in one course of 44 [R71].
cells.interpretation: [I] Personalisation scales with automation, but quality control of individual versions becomes the limiting factor in large cohorts.
cells.conflicts: R94 claims a scalable framework but its maximum class size was 30 [R94].
cells.cohort_note: Small (<50): hand-designed personalised or contextualised tasks are workable [R94], [R71]. Medium (50-200): a different topic per student has been run with 88 students [R15]. Large (>200): needs automated generation or questioning, tested with over 250 students [S156], with difficulty calibration and platform capacity as risks [R89].

cells.literature: [L] Redesigning assessments and marking multiple drafts were constrained by time and hiring freezes [R24], and design-based measures were said to demand substantial teacher time [S105]; R04 lists workload pressure as an implementation challenge [R04]. LLM question generation was claimed to cut administrative time by 68%, but the results give only a qualitative quote [R89].
cells.interpretation: [I] Personalisation shifts burden to preparation, difficulty calibration and marking divergent work; automation may reduce it but this is unproven.
cells.conflicts: R89's workload claim differs between abstract and results [R89]; no study measured staff time.

cells.literature: [L] Contextualisation was the most common adaptation in practice: departments mostly changed task requirements, such as context-specific prompts, rather than task types, which needed academic board approval [R24]. Personalised designs ran in real modules for one to two semesters, including an 88-student module [R15], [R20]. Cost falls mainly on staff time and, for tool-based variants, on platforms: AI-resistant variants needed a purpose-built programming environment [R71], per-student generation used a custom platform built on Firebase, Streamlit, React and the Piston API [R89], and automated viva questioning used Streamlit, LangChain, FAISS and ChatGPT [S156]. On licences, one design required tools that are free to students [R15], while another suggested institutions provide premium access [R20].
cells.interpretation: [I] Low-tech contextualisation is feasible within existing structures at little cost, while tool-based variants need platforms, skills and possibly licences; cost evidence is limited, because no study reported staff hours or platform or licence costs in money terms.
cells.conflicts: Design-based measures are said to demand substantial teacher time [S105], and the one workload claim for automated generation (a 68% cut in administrative time) is not supported in the results [R89].

cells.literature: [L] Students' fairness ratings of AI-resistant tasks were divided (C4 3.48; about 60% agreed) [R71], and LLM-generated per-student questions varied in difficulty by up to 30% for seemingly identical problems [R89]. Where AI use was permitted, free versus premium tools created a perceived divide, although low-proficiency EFL students felt tools levelled the field [R20]; requiring free tools was one response [R15], [R19].
cells.interpretation: [I] Equity depends on calibrating difficulty across individual versions and on equal AI access.
cells.conflicts: No study measured outcomes for students with disabilities or anxiety in personalised tasks.

evaluation_finding: Personalised tasks are strong on authenticity and can align well with computing outcomes [R04], [R73], [R50], but personalisation of the task gives weak protection against GenAI and does not establish authorship [R73], [R15], [S208], [J3]. Their value comes from pairing them with justification, process evidence or questioning tied to the student's own work [S156], [R15], [R11].
strengths: Widely recommended as authentic and closer to real-world problem solving [R04], [R01], [R50].
Can be designed to require and assess critical evaluation of GenAI output [R15], [R20].
Simple contextualisation is a low-change adaptation within existing task types [R24].
Students reported deeper thinking and debugging when AI was less useful [R71].
limitations: Personalisation of the question is not a security measure; format features explain little of AI resistance [J3], [R73].
Personal reflections and portfolios remain open to AI misuse [S208], [R24].
A personalised artefact does not show who produced it or how AI was used [R73], [J1].
AI resistance from obscure commands depends on what current models do not know [R71].
Most evidence is conceptual, self-reported or untested [R73], [R19], [S105].
practical_considerations: Pair personalised tasks with follow-up questioning or vivas on the student's own work [S156], [R24], [R11].
Test tasks against GenAI before use [R73], [R51].
For large cohorts, automated per-student generation needs difficulty calibration, capacity planning and a supported platform [R89], [S156].
Allow staff time for preparing and marking divergent tasks [R24], [S105].
Specify AI tools that all students can access free of charge, or budget for institutional access [R15], [R20].
evidence_gaps: No study measured whether personalised tasks reduce GenAI misuse compared with standard tasks.
No study tested personalised tasks against current GenAI models with repeated prompting.
No study measured staff workload for preparing or marking personalised tasks.
No study measured effects for students with disabilities, anxiety or English as an additional language.
Evidence from large computing cohorts (>200) is limited to automated questioning [S156].
